title: Generations
sub: Gen 0, 1, 2 and the large object heap
cards/0/body:
Temporary strings, per-request objects, iterators: they live for a fraction of a second. That's why the heap is split into generations:

Gen 0: new objects.
Gen 1: survived one collection.
Gen 2: long-lived objects.

A Gen 0 collection is frequent and fast: it only looks at the young.
cards/0/deep: So a Gen 0 collection doesn't have to walk the whole heap, the CLR marks spots in older generations that got a reference to a young object in a "card table". A write barrier sets the mark on every assignment to a reference field.
cards/1/task: The temporary objects Temp1 and Temp2 should go away, while Cache makes it to Gen 2.
cards/2/q: An object is in Gen 1. A Gen 0 collection runs. What happens to it?
cards/2/options/0: Nothing: a Gen 0 collection doesn't even look at it
cards/2/explain: A collection of generation N covers generations 0 through N. It doesn't touch older ones.
cards/3/title: The LOH: the large object heap
cards/3/body:
Objects of 85,000 bytes or more, usually big arrays, go straight to a separate heap, the LOH (large object heap).

It's collected only together with Gen 2 and isn't compacted by default: moving big chunks of memory is expensive.
cards/3/deep: That's why big temporary arrays are a common cause of full collections and fragmentation. The cure is ArrayPool<T>.Shared: rent a buffer and return it. Since .NET 5 there's also the POH, a heap for pinned objects.
cards/4/task: Clear both references and get both objects removed. Which collection can handle Buffer?
cards/5/q: A byte[100_000] became garbage. Who cleans it up?
cards/5/options/2: Nobody: the LOH is never cleaned
cards/5/explain: 100,000 bytes is above the 85,000 threshold, so the array is on the LOH. And the LOH is collected together with Gen 2.
cards/6/q: What is true about generations? Select all that apply.
cards/6/options/1: Survive a collection and you move to the next generation
cards/6/options/2: A Gen 2 collection is the most expensive
cards/6/options/3: Objects in Gen 2 are never removed
cards/6/explain: Gen 2 objects do get removed, but only by a full collection, which is rare.
cards/7/q: Why doesn't a huge cache that lives for the whole program slow down frequent collections?
cards/7/options/0: It quickly lands in Gen 2, and frequent Gen 0 collections don't walk it
cards/7/options/1: The GC skips objects named Cache
cards/7/options/2: The cache lives on the stack
cards/7/explain: A long-lived object moves to Gen 2 and from then on costs frequent collections almost nothing.
cards/8/q: Is calling GC.Collect() "to clean up memory" a good idea?
cards/8/options/0: Usually not: a full collection is expensive and also promotes live objects
cards/8/options/1: Yes, it speeds the program up
cards/8/options/2: Yes, it makes the GC do less work
cards/8/explain: The GC knows when to collect. A forced collection pauses threads and makes live objects "older", which makes them more expensive to clean up later.
